To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

stereotactic body radiation therapy is a viable treatment for unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma in the setting of Child–Pough cirrhosis, but that it should be used with caution in patients with ascites.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the treatment of patients with hepatoma and severe cirrhosis, who are not eligible for liver transplantation.
the treatment of hepatocellular carcinoma in patients with Child–pugh score 8 and higher cirrhosis who are not candidates for liver transplant.
the treatment of patients with hepatoma and cirrhosis who were not candidates for liver transplantation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
stereotactic body radiation therapy is not recommended for Child–Pugh B and C cirrhotic patients with HCC.
stereotactic body radiation therapy is not an effective treatment for patients with advanced hepatocellular carcinoma.
liver stereotactic radiotherapy should not be used as the sole modality for treatment of hepatocellular carcinoma patients with Child– Pugh score 8 and higher cirrhosis.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
for Child–Pugh 8-11, stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) may be a good alternative to liver transplantation in patients who are ineligible for transplant.

for hepatocellular carcinoma in the setting of cirrhosis with a Child–Pugh classification of 8 or higher, liver stereotactic radiation is a reasonable option for local control, although survival is poor.
stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) for HCC with severe cirrhosis (Child–Pugh score of 8-11) is not recommended due to poor outcomes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
patients with Child–pugh class C cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma should not receive liver-directed radiation.
patients with hepatocelluar carcinoma and cirrhosis should be evaluated for transplant and listed for transplant when appropriate.
patients with Child– Pugh score of 10 and above should be counseled on the poor prognosis of their disease and should be considered for hospice care.
